source_text: Καὶ ἔλεγεν· Διὰ τοῦτο εἴρηκα ὑμῖν, ὅτι οὐδεὶς δύναται ἐλθεῖν πρὸς μὲ, ἐὰν μὴ ᾖ δεδομένον αὐτῷ ἐκ τοῦ Πατρός μου.» Καὶ πρὸς τῷ τέλει· «Λαβὼν οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἄρτον, καὶ εὐχαριστήσας, ἔκλασε, καὶ ἐδίδου τοῖς μαθηταῖς, καὶ εἶπε· Λάβετε, φάγετε· τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά μου τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κλώμενον· τοῦτο ποιεῖτε εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν. Καὶ λαβὼν ποτήριον, εὐχαριστήσας, ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς εἰπών· Πίετε ἐξ αὐτοῦ πάντες· τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι τὸ αἷμά μου τὸ τῆς Καινῆς Διαθήκης, τὸ περὶ πολλῶν ἐκχυνόμενον εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν.» Καὶ ὁ Ἀπόστολος· «Ὁσάκις γὰρ ἂν ἐσθίητε τὸν ἄρτον τοῦτον, καὶ τὸ ποτήριον πίνητε, τὸν θάνατον τοῦ Κυρίου καταγγέλλετε.» Τί οὖν τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα, καὶ τί τὸ παρ' αὐτῶν ὄφελος; Ἵνα, ἐσθίοντές τε καὶ πίνοντες, ἀεὶ μνημονεύωμεν τοῦ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀποθανόντος καὶ ἐγερθέντος, καὶ οὕτω παιδευθῶμεν ἀναγκαίως φυλάξαι τὸ ἀποστολικὸν ἐκεῖνο τὸ ἡμῖν δεδομένον παράγγελμα, τὸ φάσκον· «Ἡ γὰρ ἀγάπη τοῦ Χριστοῦ συνέχει ἡμᾶς, κρίναντας τοῦτο, ὅτι, εἰ εἷς ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν, ἄρα οἱ πάντες ἀπέθανον· καὶ ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν, ἵνα οἱ ζῶντες μηκέτι ἑαυτοῖς ζῶσιν, ἀλλὰ τῷ ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἀποθανόντι καὶ ἐγερθέντι.» Ὁ γὰρ ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων, δηλονότι εἰς ἀνεξάλειπτον τῆς μέχρι θανάτου ὑπακοῆς μνήμην τοῦ Δεσπότου καὶ πλάστου, καὶ δι' ἐμὲ ὅπερ ἦν τὸ πλασθὲν γεγονότος. Ἀλλ' οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἐσθίειν προστέτακται, ἀλλὰ καὶ διακρίνειν τὸ τοιοῦτον τοῦ Κυρίου παρακελευόμεθα σῶμα· δηλονότι σαρκὸς μολυσμὸν καὶ πνεύματος ἀποθεμένους, καὶ δοχεῖον τοῦ πνευματικοῦ μύρου παρασκευάσαντας, οὕτως τῇ καθαρᾷ προσεγγίσαι θυσίᾳ, ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος νῦν καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.
thought_title: Eucharist as memorial of Christ's death and call to purity
orientation: Basil is concluding his homily by quoting Jesus's words at the Last Supper and Paul's words on the Lord's Supper, then explaining that eating and drinking are a perpetual memorial of Christ's death and resurrection and require approaching the pure sacrifice with a cleansed soul.
pass_a_gloss: And he was saying: For this reason I have said to you, that no one is able to come to me, unless it has been granted to him from my Father. And near the end: Jesus therefore, having taken bread, and having given thanks, broke it, and was giving it to the disciples, and said: Take, eat; this is my body which is broken for you; do this in remembrance of me. And having taken a cup, having given thanks, he gave it to them, saying: Drink from it, all of you; for this is my blood of the New Covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins. And the Apostle: For as often as you eat this bread, and drink the cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord. What then are these words, and what is the benefit from them? That, both eating and drinking, we may always remember the one who died for us and was raised, and so we may be taught necessarily to keep that apostolic commandment given to us, which says: For the love of Christ constrains us, having judged this, that, if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for the one who died for them and was raised. For the one who eats and drinks, clearly for an indelible memory of the obedience unto death of the Master and fashioner, and who for my sake became what the formed thing was. But not simply to eat has been commanded, but also we are exhorted to discern such a body of the Lord; clearly having put away defilement of flesh and spirit, and having prepared a vessel of the spiritual ointment, so to approach the pure sacrifice, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be the glory and the power now and to the ages of ages. Amen.

choices.why: The verb here describes Jesus's action of thanksgiving over the bread and cup; the glossary reserves 'Eucharist' for the sacrament as a whole, so the verbal form is rendered literally as giving thanks.
The participle is present passive, emphasizing the body as being broken on behalf of the disciples; 'broken' preserves the physical sense of κλάω used moments earlier for the bread.
The phrase is a fixed biblical expression; capitalizing 'New Covenant' signals its status as a title for the new dispensation in Christ's blood.
The verb means to announce or declare publicly; 'proclaim' captures the liturgical and kerygmatic force of the Lord's Supper as a public declaration of Christ's death.

choices.term: τὸ ἀποστολικὸν ἐκεῖνο τὸ ἡμῖν δεδομένον παράγγελμα
choices.english: that apostolic commandment given to us
choices.why: The word παράγγελμα is a command or injunction; 'commandment' preserves the authoritative tone Basil attributes to Paul's words, and 'apostolic' marks its source.
μύρον is ointment or perfumed oil, often used of the Spirit's anointing; 'spiritual ointment' keeps the sensory image of a vessel prepared to receive the Spirit's presence.

pass_b_english: And he said: “This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted to him by my Father” (John 6:65). And near the end: “So Jesus took bread, and having given thanks, he broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said: Take, eat; this is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in remembrance of me. And he took the cup, and having given thanks, he gave it to them, saying: Drink from it, all of you. For this is my blood of the New Covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Luke 22:19-20). And the Apostle says: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:26). What then are these words, and what benefit comes from them? It is so that, as we eat and drink, we may always remember the one who died and rose for us, and so be necessarily taught to keep that apostolic commandment given to us, which says: “For the love of Christ constrains us, because we have judged this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose for them” (2 Corinthians 5:14-15). For the one who eats and drinks clearly does so for an indelible remembrance of the obedience unto death of the Master and Creator, who for my sake became what the formed thing was. But we are not commanded to eat simply; rather, we are urged to discern this body of the Lord—clearly, having put away defilement of flesh and spirit, and having prepared a vessel for the spiritual ointment, so to approach the pure sacrifice, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and dominion now and to the ages of ages. Amen.

problems.quote: who for my sake became what the formed thing was
problems.source_quote: καὶ δι' ἐμὲ ὅπερ ἦν τὸ πλασθὲν γεγονότος
problems.why: Misreads syntax: Christ became what the creature (I) was, not 'what the formed thing was' abstractly.
problems.fix: who for my sake became what the formed thing was [i.e., became human like me]

edits.old: who for my sake became what the formed thing was
edits.new: who for my sake became what I, the formed thing, was

fixed: The English 'who for my sake became what the formed thing was' is ambiguous and loses the personal reference of 'δι' ἐμὲ' (for my sake) and 'τὸ πλασθὲν' (the formed thing, i.e., the human creature). The source says Christ became what the formed thing was for my sake, meaning he became human like me. The edit clarifies the personal reference without changing the meaning.

problems.quote: who for my sake became what I, the formed thing, was
problems.source_quote: καὶ δι' ἐμὲ ὅπερ ἦν τὸ πλασθὲν γεγονότος
problems.why: The Greek says the Creator became what the formed thing was, not 'for my sake became what I...was'.
problems.fix: who for my sake became what the formed thing was

problems.ruling: Source quotes John 6:65 exactly: 'Διὰ τοῦτο εἴρηκα ὑμῖν' matches 6:65, not 6:44.

problems.ruling: ἀναγκαίως adverbially modifies παιδευθῶμεν ('be taught'), not φυλάξαι ('keep'); 'keep necessarily' misreads syntax.

dismissed.quote: who for my sake became what the formed thing was
dismissed.why: The Greek says 'and for my sake became what the formed thing was'—but the English 'who for my sake became what the formed thing was' misrepresents the syntax. The participles ἀποθανόντος and ἐγερθέντος and γεγονότος all modify τοῦ Δεσπότου καὶ πλάστου. The English makes 'who... became' a relative clause, but the Greek has 'the Master and Creator, who died and rose, and for my sake became what the formed thing was.' The meaning is substantially the same though. Let me check more carefully.
dismissed.note: The checker admits the meaning is the same, and its proposed fix is identical to the current text.

dismissed.why: The Greek παρακελευόμεθα is 'we are commanded/urged,' but the syntax is 'we are commanded to discern the Lord's body.' However, the English 'urged' is weaker than 'commanded.' More importantly, the Greek has 'discern' (διακρίνειν), which the English renders correctly. But 'urged' vs 'commanded'—παρακελεύομαι can mean 'urge, exhort, command.' This is within range. Let me look again at 'having prepared a vessel for the spiritual ointment.'
dismissed.note: 'Urged' is within the normal range of παρακελεύομαι.

dismissed.quote: we are urged to discern this body of the Lord
dismissed.why: The word order in Greek emphasizes 'discern' (διακρίνειν): 'to discern such a body of the Lord we are commanded.' The English 'urged to discern this body of the Lord' changes 'such' (τοιοῦτον) to 'this' and weakens 'commanded' to 'urged.' More significantly, the Greek says 'discern such a body of the Lord'—τοιοῦτον means 'such,' not 'this.' The English 'this body' is wrong; it should be 'such a body' or 'the body in this way.' This changes the sense from 'discern in this manner' to identifying 'this body.'
dismissed.note: With the article, τὸ τοιοῦτον points back to the body just described, so 'this body' is fine, and 'urged' is acceptable.
